div.p: This paper presents a temporal characterization of the IEC 61131-3 standard for automation software. The final goal is to apply schedulability analysis to industrial distributed control systems to assure they meet timing non functional requirements. This characterization has been performed in the context of a Model Driven Design approach previously proposed by the authors. The approach defines three Domain Specific Models: control specification and hardware and software architectures. The software model uses the PLCopen XML interface for expressing IEC 61131-3 automation projects. The information contained in the whole application model is processed to generate the temporal model of the application. Schedulability analysis is achieved by generating the temporal model of the well-known Modeling and Analysis Suite for Real-Time Applications, MAST.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Industrial control systems are specific computer systems not only because of the special characteristics of the environment they control (industrial processes) but also because they use specific equipment, such as Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs), industrial communication systems (fieldbus), and dedicated I/O devices. On the other hand, as a computer system, its design deals with the definition of the software architecture. Traditionally, each control equipment vendor offered a development system based on proprietary software architectures and programming languages. In the last years, a great effort is being made by international organizations for promoting the use of standards for this field of applications. The mission of PLCopen [1] is to be the leading association resolving topics related to control programming to support the use of international standards in this field. The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) promotes open systems to be used in the industrial control field. It is composed by a set of Technical Committees (TC). In particular the TC 6 defines a common language for transferring the graphical information that appears in the screen among IEC 61131-3 compliant tools. The IEC 61131-3 standard [2] proposes a software model and programming languages for Industrial Process Measurement and Control Systems (IPMCS). Most of the PLC manufacturers are moving towards becoming IEC 61131-3 standard compliant. Related to the distributed IPMCS, the evolving IEC 61499 standard [3] is being discussed as a successor of the IEC 61131 standard. Several groups focus their research on this topic. For instance, [4] discusses the role of the IEC 61499 in factory automation and it analyzes the current on going research by several groups.

On the other hand, there are PLC based control systems in which it is necessary to assure response times of a set of activities [5]. This kind of applications commonly are characterized by a cyclic part that represents the control logic and a set of timed loops that must be executed within a specific frame time (periodic task) or triggered by a specific event (sporadic task). All of them can be characterized, from a temporal point of view, by their best, average and worst case execution times. Optionally, they can have a maximum deadline requirement, i.e. restrictions on their maximum response time. A response time is the time passed since the event occurs till its associated action is performed.

If the industrial control system is distributed, controllers may need to communicate among them and/or with I/O devices. In such a case, additional time requirements may appear, such as maximum latency for sending and receiving messages or end-to-end deadlines [6].
To assure that under all circumstances the temporal requirements are met within a concurrent architecture, where a set of tasks are scheduled, it is convenient to perform schedulability analysis.

Nowadays, there are several schedulability analysis tools that perform timing analysis having as input a temporal model of the application. In particular, MAST (Modeling and Analysis Suite for Real Time Applications) is an open source set of tools that enables engineers developing real-time applications to check the timing behavior of their application, including schedulability analysis for checking hard timing requirements [7]. Besides offering a complete set of timing analysis, it is a model based approach that uses a very rich representation of the real time system. But as far as authors know, there exists no model based analysis tools specifically designed for industrial control systems. This work falls on the engineer that designs the system based on his/her experience.

This paper proposes an approach to timing analysis of industrial control systems that relies on the model based paradigm. Section 2 briefly presents the model based approach previously proposed by the authors [8] that is composed by three domain models plus one more that describes the mappings among them. The application model is enriched in order to capture timing characteristics. Section 3 is dedicated to the generation of the MAST model. Finally, the conclusions.

div.head: 3+1 View Models of Industrial Control Systems
div.p: The design of distributed industrial control applications involves different domain fields. Each domain defines a different view of the same system: the control engineering domain defines the functional design that contains the control strategies ("what" the control system has to do in order to meet the functional and non-functional requirements). The electronicelectric engineering domain deals with the selection of the equipment needed to start-up the control system. Finally, the software engineering domain deals with the software architecture which implements the functional specifications. It defines the software architecture of the application following the software model of the IEC 61131 standard [9]. These two latter views of the system define the implementation issues ("how" to develop the functional specification). Furthermore, given that all of them represent the same application, they are not completely independent and to assure consistency, the elements of the different views must meet some relationships.

div.head: The Control Engineering view
div.p: The functional specification of an industrial control system contains the control strategies to be implemented that assure that the system under design fulfilled the functional and non-functional requirements. In order to describe a functional specification in a component based approach, the following elements are needed: (1) a hierarchy of components, where every component groups the control application functionality or part of it. It is characterized by its hierarchical level. (2) A connector represents the relationship between two components.

(3) A channel groups a set of connectors that come from or go to the same component (4) A port represents the point in which channels are related to components. Finally (5) A transaction is defined from the data read from process inputs to the data sent to process outputs having specific timing attributes in terms of period/separation and possibly a deadline. It involves a set of functional components that will be implemented as a set of POUs in the software model. It can be characterized as periodic of period T or by the event that triggers the transaction and the minimal inter-arrival time between two consecutive events. Optionally, it can have an end-to-end deadline.

div.head: The Electronic-Electric Engineering view
div.p: The hardware architecture commonly consists of a set of network nodes (nodes) connected through a set of network segments (buses). A Node element is connected to a network segment through a communication board. This view is described in two levels. The first level defines the nodes interconnected by bus segments, while the second describes the modules and boards that compose each node itself.

Related to timing attributes, each processor is characterized by its capacity and processing speed with respect to a reference speed. And every single CPU of the processing node is characterized by the run time scheduling policy (Fixed Priority, EDF, etc.) and the data access protocol (BIP, PCP or IPCP) it uses.

div.head: The Software Engineering view
div.p: The software model describes the implementation of the functional specification. It follows the IEC 61131 standard software model. The standard provides different elements that allow defining the software architecture. A Configuration represents a PLC or Open PLC, the Resource provides support for program execution (a CPU or a Virtual machine), and Tasks allow the designer to define the execution rates of different parts of the program. Finally, POUs (Program Organization Units) are the elements that provide software reuse. They define and/or use Variables, characterized by their visibility, type and value.

The characteristics defined by the IEC 61131-3 standard of both elements, POUs and tasks, have been extended with timing attributes. Originally the Task element is characterized by its priority, if it is periodic (of period T) or if it is triggered by an event. An optional deadline, not included by the standard, has been added. The characterization of POUs has been also enriched with the execution time that can be defined by the WCET (Worst Case Execution Time), the ACET (Average Case Execution Time) and the BCET (Best Case Execution Time). All of them with respect to the reference processor. Thus, the exact execution time depends on the relative processor speed.

div.head: RelationShips among views
div.p: The three domains commented above are not independent, as they define the same system from different points of view. In order to define a consistent application, their elements are related.

A transaction defined in the functional view is related to a task in the software view and, as a consequence, the POUs that implement the transaction are the POUs associated to the corresponding task.
A configuration in the software view corresponds to a PLC, i.e. a processing node in the hardware architecture.

On the other hand, the data stored in I/O boards of the hardware architecture corresponds to global variables in the software architecture. Note that the event input within a transaction is mapped to a global variable in a configuration and to an input of an I/O board.

A Markup Language (ML) containing the three domain views plus the relationship view has been developed. In particular, the software view is defined by an extended PLCopen XML interface containing the timing attributes commented above. This modeling approach is the core of an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) that supports the development cycle. Thus, during the development cycle, the model of the application is being generated by the set of heterogeneous tools integrated in the IDE [8].

div.head: Schedulability Analysis of Industrial Control Systems
div.p: Once the characterization of the three models has been extended with timing characteristics, it is necessary to analyze how they map to the model of the analysis tool. In this paper, the MAST analysis tool is used.

The following subsections present the temporal model that results from extending the Software model (the PLCopen XML interface), from the Control Engineering and from the Electronic-Electric Engineering models. Finally, the last subsection details the automatic generation of the MAST model that derives from the temporal model.

Any MAST model has a root XML element called MAST_MODEL. They are flat models as all elements of a MAST description are children of the root XML element. As an example, a Primary Scheduler is characterized by a name, the host to which it belongs to and the scheduling policy (Fixed Priority, EDF or FP_Packet).

div.head: Real-Time characterization of Industrial Control Systems
div.p: In this section, an extension of the characteristics of the elements defined in PLCopen interface is proposed in order to add the timing attributes. Figure 1 illustrates the general structure that a software model must follow in PLCopen XML interface.

The characterizations of the elements POU instance, Resource and Task have been extended as commented in Section 2.3: POU instances are enriched with the execution time in terms of WCET, ACET and/or BCET; Tasks with Deadline and the Configuration with the corresponding processing node speed.
Finally, global variables accessed by POU instances belonging to different tasks are enriched with the shared attribute for identifying them as shared resources.

Once the PLCopen XML interface has been extended with timing issues and in order to generate the input for the specific schedulability analysis tool, it is necessary to map the PLCopen enriched elements to the model elements in the time-analysis tool. The transformation rules between MAST elements and PLCopen XML elements are summarized in Table 1.

div.head: Figure 1. Extended PLCopen XML schema
div.p: A Configuration in the software model corresponds to a Processing Resource. The Resource is mapped to a Scheduler. Note that for PLCs having a unique CPU the Processing speed, the scheduling policy and the data access protocol are inherited by all the resources within the configuration. A Task corresponds to a Scheduling Server, as it organizes the execution of POUs instances that are involved in the Activities of a Transaction.

The POU instances related to a Task in the software model correspond to the Operations within the Scheduling Server. These POUs can share resources (global variables) with other POUs in different tasks. Thus, a task in the software model references to the Shared Resources their POU instances access and the WCET of the access.

div.head: Automatic generation of the MAST model
div.p: Once the mapping rules between the MAST model and the extended PLCopen model have been identified and both models are expressed in XML, the transformation rules can be implemented as an XML stylesheet [10]. XML stylesheets allow filtering and processing XML documents by means of templates.

The PLCopen2MAST.xsl XML stylesheet contains a template match for each mapping rule (see Table 1). The skeleton of the PLCopen2MAST.xsl XML stylesheet is composed by a ppx:project template that acts as the main function. The goal of this template is to generate the root of the MAST model and to invoke the rest of templates. The aim of the ppx:task template is to generate the scheduling server and to collect all needed information associated to a MAST task. The ppx:resource template generates the processing resource. Finally, with the ppx:global_var the shared global variables are transformed in shared resources.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: The work presented here applies the MDE concepts in the Industrial Automation field. Three different views have been identified as the domains involved in the design of such type of systems: control engineering view, electronic-electric engineering view and software engineering. During the development cycle of such type of applications, independent and heterogeneous tools participate. These three views have been defined making use of XML schema metamodelling language, and they constitute the core of an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) to which different COTS tools could be integrated. The characteristics of these three views have been extended in order to achieve the integration of a schedulability analysis tool to the IDE. Ongoing work includes to analyse and to compare the results of different mappings between Industrial Control Systems and MAST models.
